cases.interviewerQuestion: Bearer-token auth for the extension since cookies couldn't cross domains—what did that mean for session management and token refresh compared to how the main app handled auth, and did that difference ever bite you in production?
cases.tonyRaw: The main app could lean on cookie-based sessions since everything lived on the same domain, but the extension runs in its own context so that was never an option — bearer tokens were the only real path. That meant I had to build out token issuance and refresh as an explicit part of the extension's API surface rather than getting it for free from the browser, and think about token lifetime tradeoffs differently since a stale or expired token in the extension fails silently in a popup rather than redirecting a browser tab to a login page. I don't have a specific production incident to point to from this, but that class of bug — auth failing quietly in a small UI surface instead of loudly in a full page — was exactly the kind of thing I was watching for when building out the CRUD proxying and onboarding flow, since it's the failure mode that costs you the most debugging time if it does hit.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What made a single undifferentiated store untenable here — was there a specific stale-state or re-render bug that exposed the need to split things into three layers rather than just patching the existing store?
cases.tonyRaw: The pattern that broke things was treating collaborative document state, server-persisted state, and local UI state as if they had the same lifecycle and could live in one store. They don't — the collaborative layer needs to reconcile with other clients in real time, the server layer needs cache invalidation semantics, and the UI layer just needs to react to user input, and mashing those together meant a change in one would trigger re-renders or stale reads in places that had no business caring about it. I didn't isolate it down to one dramatic bug I can point to, but the class of it was consistent: components reading document state would occasionally render against a value that hadn't caught up with a server invalidation, or presence updates would cause re-renders in components only tied to local UI state. Splitting into Liveblocks for the collaborative layer, TanStack Query for server state, and Context/reducer for local UI state solved it because each layer got a lifecycle model that actually matched what it was managing, instead of patching symptoms in a single store that was doing three jobs at once.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You had to support two concurrent editor versions while integrating AI output into ProseMirror's typed node model. What made that dual-version support painful in practice, and did it shape how you designed the state-management layer?
cases.tonyRaw: I co-led a team of 3 to 4 engineers on that feature, and I personally designed the state-management layer that integrated AI output into our editor's document model. The dual-version support was painful because the two editor versions didn't share the same typed node shape, so AI output that mapped cleanly onto one document model could violate assumptions in the other — you couldn't just write one transform and trust it everywhere. That constraint pushed the state-management layer toward being more defensive than I'd have designed in a single-version world: validating and normalizing AI output against whichever document model it was landing in, rather than assuming a single canonical shape. It made the layer more complex up front, but it meant we weren't shipping version-specific hacks that would have been a maintenance problem later.

cases.interviewerQuestion: How did you go about validating that the ported calculations matched the original TypeORM implementation exactly, especially for those high-volume trader accounts?
cases.tonyRaw: I worked on porting our trade metric computation from the TypeORM-based implementation into the new GraphQL API architecture, and the validation piece was really about working with stakeholders who understood the original calculations well enough to catch discrepancies I might miss. High-volume trader accounts mattered specifically because that's where edge cases in the math tend to surface — enough trades that rounding, ordering, or aggregation differences actually compound into visible drift instead of staying hidden in the noise. So rather than trusting the port in isolation, I leaned on comparing outputs against the existing implementation for those accounts and treating any mismatch as a signal to go find where the logic diverged. It wasn't a formal test suite I owned end to end, it was iterative reconciliation with people who knew what the numbers should look like.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You spent nine months iterating on the debounce delay and timing for the autosave hook — what made that tuning so hard to settle, and what signals told you the current value was wrong before you'd adjust it again?
cases.tonyRaw: The hard part wasn't finding one magic number, it was that the right delay depended on what the user was actually doing — fast typing needed a longer debounce so we weren't saving mid-thought, but switching away from the editor needed a much shorter window so nothing got lost. The signal that told me a value was wrong was usually save frequency relative to actual edit-worthy pauses: if saves were firing while someone was clearly still typing, the delay was too short, and if I saw dirty state sitting unsaved longer than felt safe, it was too long. I owned that tuning solo over about nine months on the artifact editor, wiring it through dirty-state tracking rather than raw keystroke timing, since dirty state was a more honest signal of "there's something worth saving" than time alone. A teammate later reworked the editor-specific hook further after I'd rotated off, but that stale-closure and grace-period refinement was a separate pass, not part of the original tuning problem I was solving.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Before engineering you were an occupational therapist. Are you still licensed for that? I ask because I am curious whether the clinical background shaped how you approached the state architecture.
cases.tonyRaw: To answer directly: no, I'm not currently licensed, that was a past career before I moved into engineering. As for the state architecture, that came from working through the actual bug class rather than any clinical carryover — we had one undifferentiated store handling realtime collaborative data, server-persisted data, and local UI state together, and that mixing was causing stale-state and re-render bugs. I solo-owned splitting it into three layers: Liveblocks for the collaborative document state with typed LiveObject/LiveList and presence, TanStack Query for server state and cache invalidation, and a Context/reducer layer for local UI state. Once each layer only had to reason about its own kind of data, that whole class of bugs mostly went away.

cases.interviewerQuestion: By what percentage did your chunking strategy improve reliability on long meetings?
cases.tonyRaw: I don't have a percentage to give you, so I won't make one up. What I can tell you is the design: try the full transcript first and only chunk when you actually hit context-window overflow, and when you do chunk, break at sentence or speaker boundaries instead of a fixed character cutoff. That mattered because a naive fixed-length cutoff would split mid-sentence or mid-turn, which degrades whatever the model does with that chunk downstream — breaking on natural boundaries kept each chunk semantically coherent.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Since you were shaping the data model as a team, what was the trickiest tradeoff you argued over — something where the GraphQL schema and the underlying data model pulled in different directions?
cases.tonyRaw: I was part of a team that built the Trader Public Profile platform — I contributed to the data model design and helped build the GraphQL API layer and React UI, but this wasn't a feature I owned end to end, so I want to be careful not to claim credit for the specific resolution of that tradeoff since it was argued out as a group. What I can speak to is the general shape of the tension: the underlying data model was organized around how the data was actually produced and stored, while the GraphQL schema needed to present something clean and stable for the client. Those two pressures don't naturally agree, and any time you flatten the schema for the frontend's convenience you risk baking in assumptions that make the underlying model harder to evolve later. I'd rather point you to someone who drove that specific decision than reconstruct an argument I was one voice in.
